lessons.title: Demand and Rate Cyclicals: Autos, Real Estate, Capital Goods, and Banks

body.text: Commodity cyclicals follow global prices. Demand and rate cyclicals follow Indian wallets: how cheap the EMI is, how confident buyers feel, and whether companies and the government are willing to commit to big projects. Each has a monthly or quarterly number that tells you the turn is coming.

children.text: Autos, real estate, capital goods, and banks make up a large share of the Nifty 50 and of most Indian equity mutual funds. Unlike steel, their selling prices are not set in London or Shanghai. Their earnings rise and fall with domestic demand, interest rates, and credit. This lesson breaks down what drives each one and the specific data that shows the cycle turning before profits do.

children.text: Autos: Not One Cycle, Four

Calling autos cyclical is correct but too broad. The four main vehicle segments respond to different parts of the economy, which is why a two-wheeler maker and a truck maker can be at completely different points of their cycles in the same year.

body.caption: Auto segments and their demand drivers

cells: Freight volumes, infrastructure activity, fleet operator financing
Deepest: fleet owners can simply stop buying for a year or two
Urban incomes, car loan rates, new model launches
Moderate, heavily tied to rural health
Moderate, driven by agriculture more than GDP

markDefs.definition: Vehicles sitting with dealers that have been billed by the manufacturer but not yet sold to customers, usually measured in days of sales.

children.text: Auto investors get something rare: monthly data. Listed auto companies publish their sales volumes at the start of every month, and industry bodies publish wholesale and retail figures soon after. Watch the gap between wholesale dispatches to dealers and retail sales to customers. When manufacturers keep pushing vehicles to dealers faster than customers buy them,
dealer inventory
builds up, discounts rise, and production cuts usually follow. That build-up is often the first sign of a downturn.
The EMI Effect

Most Indian cars and homes are bought on loans, so buyers think in EMIs, not in sticker prices. A rate change that looks small on paper changes affordability meaningfully, especially for home loans with long tenures.

body.caption: P = loan amount, r = annual interest rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100, n = number of monthly instalments

children.text: Try it: enter a ₹8 lakh car loan over 5 years at 9%, then at 11%. The EMI moves from about ₹16,607 to about ₹17,394. For a car, the rate effect is modest. For a 20-year home loan, it is large enough to push buyers out of a budget bracket entirely, which is why real estate is more rate-sensitive than autos.
Real Estate: A Long Cycle Where Reported Profit Lags

markDefs.definition: The value of new property bookings made by customers in a period, regardless of when the developer will recognise that sale as revenue in its accounts.

children.text: Real estate cycles are long, often running seven to ten years from one peak to the next, because projects take years to build and unsold inventory takes years to clear. Indian listed developers generally recognise revenue in their P&L only as projects are completed and handed over, so reported profit can look strong years after demand has turned, or weak while bookings are booming. The number that tracks the cycle in real time is
pre-sales
, which most large developers disclose every quarter in their investor presentations.

body.title: What Tells You Where a Developer Is in the Cycle

columns.label: Leading signals
points: Pre-sales value and volume, quarter on quarter
Collections from customers, which fund construction
New project launches and how quickly they sell
Unsold inventory relative to annual sales

columns.label: Lagging signals
points: Reported revenue and net profit in the P&L
P/E ratio, which is distorted by lumpy project completions
Annual growth rates calculated from reported earnings

body.text: Real estate adds a balance sheet trap on top of the cycle. Developers that borrow heavily to buy land in a boom face rising interest costs and falling sales at the same time when the cycle turns. In the long slump after 2008, many heavily indebted Indian developers struggled for a decade. Always check net debt alongside pre-sales.

children.text: Capital Goods: Living Off the Order Book

Capital goods and engineering companies earn revenue by executing large, multi-year contracts: power equipment, metro systems, refineries, factories. That makes the order book the heart of the analysis. Orders won today become revenue over the next two to four years. In a downturn, revenue keeps flowing from old orders while new orders dry up, which is exactly why this group is a late cyclical. Two demand sources matter: government capex, announced in the Union Budget every year, and private capex, which usually picks up only when existing factories are running close to full capacity.

body.caption: Roughly how many years of revenue the current orders represent

body.title: Read the Order Book
body.prompt: An engineering company has an order book of ₹36,000 crore and revenue of ₹12,000 crore over the last 12 months. What is its book-to-bill ratio?
body.explanation: 36,000 / 12,000 = 3.0x, about three years of revenue visibility. But visibility is not safety. Check the trend: if order inflows each quarter are falling below revenue, the order book is shrinking and growth will slow in a year or two. Also check whether contracts are fixed-price, because a spike in steel or copper prices can squeeze margins on orders already won.

children.text: Banks: The Rate Cycle and the Credit Cycle

markDefs.definition: Loan loss provisions for a period divided by average loans, expressed as a percentage. It shows how much of the loan book a bank is setting aside for bad loans.

children.text: Banks ride two cycles at once. The rate cycle moves their net interest margin, the gap between what they earn on loans and pay on deposits. The credit cycle moves their
credit cost
. Of the two, credit cost is by far the bigger swing factor. A bank's pre-provision profit is fairly stable; what destroys earnings is a wave of bad loans.

body.caption: Illustrative bank: ₹1,00,000 crore loan book, pre-provision operating profit of ₹2,500 crore (2.5% of loans)

body.title: Illustrative Bank PBT at Different Credit Costs (₹ crore)

children.text: India lived through exactly this. Loans made to steel, power, and infrastructure companies during the 2000s capex boom turned bad in the following decade. The gross NPA ratio of Indian scheduled commercial banks rose above 11% by March 2018, and many public sector banks reported losses. After years of clean-up, recoveries, and a shift towards retail lending, gross NPAs fell below 3% by 2024, and bank profits hit records. Same banks, opposite ends of the credit cycle.

body.title: Why rising rates can briefly help bank margins

children.text: Since October 2019, new floating-rate retail and MSME loans in India have had to be linked to an external benchmark, most commonly the RBI repo rate. When the RBI raises rates, these loans reprice quickly. Deposits, especially fixed deposits, reprice only as they mature. For a few quarters, loan yields rise faster than deposit costs and NIMs expand. The reverse happens when rates are cut: loan yields fall quickly while deposit costs stay high, compressing margins.
The catch: if rates stay high long enough, borrowers start to struggle, and credit costs rise later. Rate cycles move margins in quarters. Credit cycles move profits in years.

NBFCs add one more layer: funding. Banks have deposits, but NBFCs borrow from banks, mutual funds, and bond markets. When IL&FS defaulted in 2018, funding markets froze for many NBFCs, and even companies with good loan books saw their stocks crash because investors feared they could not refinance. For NBFCs, liquidity is part of the cycle.

body.title: Which Signal Comes First?
body.question: You want early warning that a housing downcycle may be starting. Which data point is most useful?
options: A developer's reported annual net profit
A fall in quarterly pre-sales and slower sales at new launches across several developers
The developer's P/E ratio compared with the Nifty 50
body.explanation: Reported profit follows project completions and can lag demand by years, making P/E and dividends lagging too. Pre-sales and launch absorption across multiple developers show what buyers are doing right now.

body.title: The Balanced-Looking Portfolio
body.scenario: Meera, a mutual fund investor, holds a banking and financial services fund, an infrastructure fund, and a direct holding in a large housing developer. The RBI has raised rates several times over the past year. Her banking fund has done well because bank margins expanded. She plans to add more to it, reasoning that higher rates are good for banks.
body.prompt: What is Meera overlooking about the cycles in her portfolio?
body.modelAnswer: Meera is reading a short-term rate cycle effect as a permanent benefit. Bank margins often expand in the first few quarters of rate hikes because floating-rate loans reprice faster than deposits, but that effect fades as deposit costs catch up. If rates stay high, stress builds among borrowers and credit costs rise later, which hits profits much harder than margins helped. Meanwhile her housing developer is directly hurt by higher home loan EMIs, and her infrastructure fund is exposed to capex slowing if borrowing costs deter projects. All three holdings are rate and credit cyclicals. Adding more to the banking fund concentrates her in the same cycle rather than diversifying it.

body.title: Your Demand and Rate Cyclical Data Calendar
steps: First few days of every month: listed auto companies' sales volumes, with retail registration data following
Every RBI Monetary Policy Committee meeting: repo rate decision and stance, for autos, real estate, and banks
Every quarter: developers' pre-sales and collections from investor presentations
Every quarter: capital goods order inflows, order book, and book-to-bill from results
Every quarter: bank loan growth, NIM, GNPA, and credit cost from results
Every February: Union Budget capital expenditure allocation, for capital goods and infrastructure
Every six months: RBI Financial Stability Report for system-wide asset quality trends

body.label: Reserve Bank of India
body.description: Monetary policy statements, the Financial Stability Report, and data on bank credit growth and asset quality.

points: Demand and rate cyclicals follow domestic EMIs, confidence, and capex rather than global commodity prices
Autos are four cycles: commercial vehicles are deepest, while two-wheelers and tractors follow rural incomes and the monsoon
Home loan EMIs make real estate highly rate-sensitive; track pre-sales, not reported profit, which lags by years
Capital goods live off their order book; falling order inflows warn of slowing growth well before revenue drops
Banks ride the rate cycle through margins and the credit cycle through credit costs, and credit costs are the bigger swing
NBFCs add a funding and liquidity cycle on top of the credit cycle

body.text: The bank, engineering company, loan examples, and Meera's scenario are illustrative. Industry statistics are rounded from RBI and public sources and should be checked against the latest releases. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security or fund.
